title: Microburst benchmark log — KV cache warmup & short bursts
content:
Objective:
Run focused microburst experiments to understand p95/p99 behavior when KV cache is cold vs warmed and when client-side batching is disabled. Looking specifically at 64-token responses and sub-second latency targets (aim: p95 < 200ms for 1-3 concurrent requests; p99 < 350ms ideally).

Context / motivation:
- Customers see sudden spikes (e.g., feature flagged rollouts, traffic spikes from a single user) and Redwood needs predictable tail latency even for short requests.
- Previous throughput tests cover steady-state long streams; microbursts expose different code paths: new KV allocations, attention buffer init, GPU kernel overhead for short seqs.
- Hypothesis: KV cache warmup and small batch sizes cause disproportionate p99 spikes due to per-request kernel launch overhead and runtime arbitration.

Experimental setup (env):
- Model: redwood-alpha-7b-v2 (FP16, fast-kernels profile)
- Hardware: Dedicated dev node g4dn-like; 1x A100-40GB (dev pool), CUDA 12.1, cuBLAS-XT off, kernel tuning: default
- Runtime: serve v3.6.1 (local dev cluster), batching disabled for these runs (continuous_batching=false), prefix/KV cache controlled by tests
- Client: synthetic load generator (go-based) that can issue precise bursts and vary concurrency; client RTT ~ <1ms inside same AZ
- Request: prompt template small: "Summarize in one sentence: <input>" -> target gen length 64 tokens average
- Metrics captured: latency per request (ms), CPU/GPU util, kernel launch counts, KV cache hits, queue depth, and per-request trace id for correlation

Test matrix: (each run = 15k requests over 10min with microburst injection every 10s)
- A: Cold KV, no priming, concurrency 1 (single requester bursts of 3 concurrent requests), batching off
- B: Warm KV (1000 prime requests), concurrency 1, batching off
- C: Cold KV, concurrency 3 steady (3 parallel clients), batching off
- D: Warm KV, concurrency 3 steady, batching off
- E: Warm KV + client-side tiny batching (group 2) to check tradeoffs

Raw summary results (aggregated):
- A (cold, bursts 1-3 concurrent): p50=68ms, p95=212ms, p99=498ms, max=920ms
- B (warmed): p50=62ms, p95=128ms, p99=214ms, max=310ms
- C (cold, steady 3): p50=95ms, p95=300ms, p99=710ms, max=1250ms
- D (warm, steady 3): p50=82ms, p95=170ms, p99=290ms, max=450ms
- E (warm + client batch 2): p50=72ms, p95=140ms, p99=240ms, max=350ms

Observations / quick interpretations:
- Warm KV dramatically reduces tail (p99) by ~2x-3x across burst and steady scenarios. The biggest gains are for p99 and max (top 1% of requests) which suggests most overhead is cold allocation/initialization cost.
- Cold microbursts (A/C) show p99 > 400ms which fails our 350ms soft target. Warmed scenarios B/D/E are within or near soft targets.
- Steady concurrency of 3 increases median by ~20-35ms compared to single-concurrency warm runs. Some of that is GPU occupancy/context switching, not the KV cache.
- Tiny client-side batching (E) didn't materially hurt median and reduced p99 slightly vs D. So in production some small request coalescing might be beneficial without hurting latency SLOs.

Correlated signals (from traces):
- High-latency traces often show a spike in "kv-init" span (50-300ms) for cold runs. Following spans (kernel exec) remain similar across cold/warm.
- Kernel launch count is higher per request in cold runs (additional short kernels to allocate attention buffers).
- GPU utilization low (<20%) for 64-token runs; this implies kernel startup overhead dominates, not compute.

Representative trace snippet (cold p99) - simplified timeline (ms):
- 0   client send
- 4   receive request on worker
- 6   allocate KV buffers (+120ms)
- 130 load model weights into cache (fast path)
- 150 kernel launch (attn) -> 60ms
- 220 assembly/serialize -> 40ms
- 260 response sent

Small ascii table of p95/p99 (for quick paste):
Scenario, p95(ms), p99(ms)
Cold burst, 212, 498
Warm burst, 128, 214
Cold steady-3, 300, 710
Warm steady-3, 170, 290
Warm + batch2, 140, 240

Immediate conclusions:
- KV cache warmup is the dominant knob for tail in microbursts. We should prioritize fast priming or cheap async priming strategy for cold clients.
- Short-term mitigation: recommend client-side warmup (on onboarding volume), or server-side async priming for new model shards when traffic arrives from a customer.
- Longer-term: reduce per-request kernel launch overhead path for short sequences (investigate fused kernels or persistent buffer pools).

Actionable next steps / TODOs:
- [ ] Run same microburst tests on a 2x GPU node to see if multi-GPU scheduling changes behavior (assign to @Aisha)
- [ ] Prototype async priming: when a new shard is created, enqueue a set of lightweight priming requests (10 x 16-token) to fill KV structures (assign to @Evan)
- [ ] Measure memory allocator impact: try persistent KV slab allocator (patch branch: perf/kv-slab) and re-run cold tests (me, Ryan)
- [ ] Add a microburst scenario job to CI that runs once per week against staging (low-cost smoke check)

Notes to self / open questions:
- What is the cost impact of always doing a small async prime (idle GPU ops)? Need cost estimate (GPU minutes per week) vs decreased p99 SLA penalties.
- Is there a generic signal we can use to detect "new shard" vs "already active" to trigger priming automatically without owner intervention? Should tie to shard last-active timestamp.
- Check interaction with quantized kernels (int8) — might have different init costs.

Attachments / artifacts to produce next:
- Lightweight svg chart: p95/p99 vs scenario (for slides)
- Example traces (zip) for warm vs cold p99 to attach to RFC
- Small script to reproduce locally (will push to GH linked PR above)

Experiment notes (raw run IDs):
- run-20260301-microburst-A (cold bursts) -> logs: /tmp/run-20260301-A.log
- run-20260302-B-warm -> logs: /tmp/run-20260302-B.log
- run-20260303-C-steady3 -> logs: /tmp/run-20260303-C.log

If I get time today: try warm priming with only KV allocations (avoid full forward pass) to see if we can reduce priming cost further.

End of notes.
